opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what I believe actually has impact. When I was in undergrad at Tsinghua, I looked around at the reinforcement learning field and saw a lot of papers, but when you actually tried to reproduce them, the code was either missing, broken, or so messy that you couldn't build on it. A paper might get cited, but very often nobody really uses it. A good open-source library, on the other hand, is something people touch every day. They run it, they file issues, they build their own research on top of it. To me that's a much more direct and honest signal that you've created something valuable.

So with Tianshou, my goal was: can I make an RL framework that's clean, fast, modular, and actually pleasant to use? If people star it, fork it, and contribute back, that means it's solving a real problem for them. A three-digit, and later four-digit, star count isn't the point in itself, but it's feedback from real users rather than from three reviewers.

There's also a personal side. I'm an engineer at heart. I enjoy writing code that's elegant and well-tested more than I enjoy polishing a paper to squeeze out half a percent on some benchmark. And honestly, I think that engineering skill turned out to matter a lot. When I later worked on things like EnvPool and then joined OpenAI, the ability to build robust infrastructure was exactly what was needed. Research progress, especially at scale, is often bottlenecked by infrastructure, not by ideas.

So it wasn't that I thought papers were useless. It's more that I asked myself what kind of contribution I wanted to leave, and I felt a widely used tool would help more people than one more paper that sits in a PDF.

r002.rationale: It says the star count was feedback rather than the point itself, but does not state that reaching three digits alone failed to satisfy his desire for a proper repository.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, honestly, back when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, I remember thinking that if I could get a repo with a hundred stars, that would be worth more to me than a paper at a top conference. And that feeling never really went away.

Part of it is just about who actually uses the thing. A paper gets read by maybe a few dozen people, and most of them skim the abstract and move on. But when I built Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, people were cloning it, opening issues, pulling it into their own projects. You get this very direct signal that you helped someone. Someone in a different country, who you'll never meet, is training an agent with code you wrote at two in the morning. That feels real in a way that a citation count doesn't.

The other part is that code has to actually work. You can write a paper where the method only works on three seeds and nobody will ever know. You cannot do that with a library. If your PPO implementation is subtly broken, someone will file an issue within a week, and they'll be right. So maintaining a repo forced me to be honest about what I understood and what I didn't. I learned way more about RL from debugging Tianshou than from reading papers about RL.

And then there's the longevity. Most papers have a half-life of about a conference cycle. A good library gets used for years. Envpool, for example, people were still picking it up long after we stopped actively pushing on it, just because it solved a real bottleneck for them.

I'd also say, and this is maybe a bit contrarian, that in this field the incentives push hard toward paper count, and I just didn't find that motivating. I'd rather have one thing that a thousand people depend on than ten papers that nobody reproduces. The star count isn't the point in itself, it's just a rough proxy for "did this matter to anyone."

astra-6.text:
For me, it was about whether the work was useful to someone else. A paper can explain an idea, but a proper GitHub repository means someone can actually run it, understand it, and build on it. That takes a different kind of effort—documentation, examples, making things work outside your own setup.

The three-digit count wasn’t really the point by itself. It represented a signal that people were interested enough to engage with what I’d built. I still cared about papers, but I wanted that connection between an idea and something people could actually use.
